course:
The positive side of the course is that it introduces students to many theoretical approaches in foreign policy analysis. However, in my opinion, the course is too heavily based on abstract theories, many of which feel very similar to IR 101 or IR Theory topics. Because of this, the course does not feel as practical or as instructive as it could be.

I think a Foreign Policy Analysis course should focus more on actual analysis. The current theory-heavy structure does not fully prepare students who may want to become policy analysts or work in related professional fields in the future. Not all students aim to become academics, so the course would be more useful if the theoretical part of the syllabus were reduced and replaced with more practical, applied content.

For example, instead of spending seminars mostly on academic articles selected by the instructor, it would be more beneficial to analyze current foreign policy events from around the world. This would help students follow international developments more actively in their daily lives and learn how to interpret them from a more professional perspective, rather than only reading about historical or theoretical cases.

In my opinion, seminars could be redesigned so that each student brings a current foreign policy news item together with a short analysis, and the class discusses these examples. This would be a more meaningful use of seminar time than focusing on a single article. It would also be fairer and more useful if students were graded on this kind of continuous analytical effort instead of being evaluated mainly through a short oral exam.

The professor’s strongest point is their strong command of mainstream International Relations theories and their ability to explain complex theoretical frameworks in a clear, structured, and systematic manner. Realism, liberalism, and constructivism were presented rigorously and with close attention to their internal logic and analytical strengths. The professor also clearly stated at the beginning of the course that the focus would be on mainstream theory and explained the rationale behind this choice, which helped set transparent expectations for students.

The weakest point is that, despite this transparency, the course’s strong emphasis on mainstream theory left limited room for engagement with critical or post-positivist perspectives. At the master’s level, where the number of courses students can take is already limited, a more integrated approach combining mainstream and critical theories within the same course could have been more efficient and beneficial for students.

The strongest aspect of the course is its systematic and rigorous coverage of mainstream International Relations theories, which provided a solid analytical foundation for understanding the discipline. The structure of the syllabus and the depth of the readings encouraged serious engagement with theoretical debates and promoted critical thinking at the master’s level.

One challenge of the course was the heavy reading load, particularly when readings were both lengthy and conceptually dense. In such cases, it could occasionally be difficult to maintain a clear sense of context during seminar discussions. Providing the discussion questions in advance might have helped students better situate the readings and organise their thoughts, especially for more complex texts. At the same time, it is understandable that sharing questions beforehand could reduce spontaneous critical engagement during class, as students would already know what to expect. Balancing these two considerations could further enhance the effectiveness of seminar discussions.

● The strongest part was, despite the potential popular opinion within the generic student community, the extremely heavy curriculum. This may be a hard slap for a first-year MA student, but the readings really show you the deep intricacies of the mainstream IR (mostly Realist schools) that are mostly dumbed down or hollowed out in scope during undergraduate education. Even though I was extremely confused and shocked throughout the whole semester by how my knowledge from my undergraduate years was partially wrong or dreadfully deficient, and how the content of the readings seemed so complex beyond my comprehension, I appreciated this very refreshing wake-up call and am extremely excited to study and conquer this field until my future graduation.
● The weakest part was that the moderation of the discussions was not really suitable for fresh graduate students, especially considering that most of these students are anxiety-driven, afraid of making mistakes when feeling judged, or more prone to imposter syndrome. I sensed that most MA students became less forthcoming in bringing their comments and points of view openly over time, because I believe that PhD students’ rigorous domination of the discussions and their way of evaluating the readings were met with and favored by the instructor’s survival-of-the-fittest metrics. This really killed my joy of actively attending the sessions, with the course ending up as a liability of “three hours to pass by” for me, which is very hard for someone like me—who really likes to be challenged—to say. For the next semesters, it would be nice to have this possibility reviewed so that fair discussion logistics are set up, with some space for expression and just a little empathy extended to MA students, so the waters could be warmer for them.

With making this mandatory and saying "the ones who want to focus on critical approaches can take x course as an elective in the future" i think we are limiting ourselves so much.
